home.title: Lizzy to Lana
home.subtitle: A Fan Archive
home.tagline: Nine eras, sixteen releases, and a small collection of photographs — a public record of Lana Del Rey's work, told in order.
home.intro: This is not a diary and it is not a news site. It is a fan-made archive: a place to follow the records, the tours, and the visual chapters without gossip, speculation, or uncredited images.

sections.introTitle: A public record, not a personal feed
introBody: This is not a diary and it is not a news site. It is a fan-made archive: a place to follow the records, the tours, and the visual chapters without gossip, speculation, or uncredited images.
Everything here is generated from one data file. A correction made once propagates to every page that uses it — and every photograph carries its creator, its source, and its licence.
sections.introAsideTitle: What you will not find here
sections.highlightsNote: A starting point for each kind of reader: the beginning, the record that changed the scale, and the chapter that is still open.
sections.galleryNote: A small selection from the eighteen credited photographs in the collection.
sections.albumsNote: Four releases that open different doors into the catalogue.

closing.title: The archive is a map, not a monument.
closing.body: Follow the eras in order, jump to the record that brought you here, or search the whole collection. Every route is a real page, and every page can be read without JavaScript.

journey.title: Nine chapters, in order
journey.lede: From a three-song EP made under the name Lizzy Grant to an unreleased country record announced under three titles: the archive follows the work, not the noise around it.
journey.note: Each chapter links to its releases and to the photographs that survive with a clear licence. Dates are release dates, not the dates a song was first performed.

gallery.title: A small, credited collection
gallery.lede: Eighteen photographs, stored locally and used under named open licences. No hotlinks, no search-engine grabs, no image without a creator and a source.
gallery.note: Filter by chapter, open any photograph for its full caption, credit, licence, and original file page. Two periods currently use a clearly marked placeholder instead of an unlicensed image.

discography.title: Sixteen releases, in order
discography.lede: Studio albums, EPs, a short film, a spoken-word record, and two releases that have been announced but not yet heard. Standard editions are listed unless noted otherwise.
discography.note: Tracklists follow the standard editions. Deluxe, retailer, and regional bonus tracks are noted in the text rather than mixed into the main list.

sources.title: Receipts, not rumours
sources.lede: Every factual claim in the archive has a reference behind it. Photographs have a separate credit list with the creator, the original file page, and the licence.
sources.note: Wikipedia is used as a finding aid, not as a final authority: its citations lead to interviews, announcements, and reviews. Date-sensitive claims are checked against the date shown on the page.

footer.note: An independent, source-led fan archive of Lana Del Rey's recorded work. Built to be read, not to harvest attention.

eras.label: Lizzy Grant
eras.title: Lizzy Grant & the early recordings
eras.summary: Before the name, the room: church choirs, school bands, Brooklyn clubs, and two records made under the name Lizzy Grant.
eras.lede: Elizabeth Woolridge Grant was born in New York City on 21 June 1985 and grew up in Lake Placid. Music came first through church and school, then through small clubs in Brooklyn and New Jersey, where she performed under names including Sparkle Jump Rope Queen and Lizzy Grant.

sections.heading: A name before the name
body: After studying philosophy at Fordham University, Grant began working with producer David Kahne. The first public document is the three-song Kill Kill EP, released in October 2008 on 5 Points Records. A debut album, Lana Del Ray, followed in January 2010.

Both records are small, strange, and unmistakably early: torch songs, trailer-park imagery, and a voice already looking for a cinematic frame. They are not the sound of a finished project, but they are the sound of one beginning.

sections.heading: The turn
body: The Lizzy Grant material did not stay in print for long, but it set the terms for what came next. The stage name changed, the production widened, and a homemade video for “Video Games” turned a private-sounding song into a public one.

The early chapter is short, but it explains the rest. The archive keeps it separate from the major-label era because the records were made under a different name, for a different scale, with a different set of expectations.

facts.label: Early aliases
facts.value: Sparkle Jump Rope Queen; Lizzy Grant; May Jailer

eras.label: Born to Die / Paradise
eras.title: Born to Die, Paradise, and the bright dark
eras.summary: A homemade video becomes a major-label debut, and the baroque-pop frame gets its first full-scale test.
eras.lede: The “Video Games” video arrived in 2011 with a homemade Super 8 quality and a chorus that felt older than the internet. By the time Born to Die was released in January 2012, the song had already changed the scale of the project.

sections.heading: A major-label debut
body: Born to Die arrived on 27 January 2012 through Stranger, Interscope, and Polydor. Its 12-track standard edition mixed baroque pop, trip hop, and widescreen strings; the deluxe edition added “Without You”, “Lolita”, and “Lucky Ones”. The album peaked at number two on the Billboard 200 and topped charts in Australia, France, Germany, and the UK, among others.

In December 2025, Billboard reported that Born to Die had become the longest-charting album by a female artist in Billboard 200 history, with 618 weeks on the chart. The record's afterlife is now part of the story.

sections.heading: Paradise and the film
body: Paradise followed in November 2012: eight tracks, including “Ride”, “American”, “Cola”, and “Gods & Monsters”, plus the iTunes bonus “Burning Desire”. The following year, the 27-minute short film Tropico threaded “Body Electric”, “Gods & Monsters”, and “Bel Air” into a three-chapter narrative.

“Young and Beautiful” (2013) and the Cedric Gervais remix of “Summertime Sadness” carried the era into film and radio. The visual language — Americana, motels, wide skies, a camera that lingers — became as recognisable as the songs.

facts.label: Key singles
facts.value: Video Games; Born to Die; Blue Jeans; Ride; Young and Beautiful

eras.label: Ultraviolence
eras.title: Ultraviolence and the guitar
eras.summary: Dan Auerbach, live guitars, and a harder, stranger record than the one before it.
eras.lede: Ultraviolence was released on 13 June 2014. After the orchestral scale of Born to Die and Paradise, the third album moved toward live guitar, desert-rock space, and a rawer vocal presence, with Dan Auerbach of the Black Keys as a central collaborator.

sections.heading: A different room
body: The album's 11-track standard edition opens with “Cruel World” and runs through “West Coast”, “Brooklyn Baby”, “Money Power Glory”, and “The Other Woman”. The writing is still cinematic, but the frame is dirtier: less string section, more room sound.

It debuted at number one in eleven countries, including the United States, and reached the top five in more than twenty territories. The deluxe edition added “Black Beauty”, “Guns and Roses”, and “Florida Kilos”; later editions added “Is This Happiness” and “Flipside”.

sections.heading: Outside the album
body: The era also produced “Big Eyes” and “I Can Fly” for Tim Burton's film Big Eyes (2014), two songs that sit comfortably beside the album's darker palette. The live shows of 2014 leaned into the same contrast: a small, almost static stage presence against a very large sound.

Ultraviolence is the chapter where the archive's idea of “era” becomes visual as well as musical. The photographs from Coachella and Rock en Seine show a performer dressed for a different kind of weather than the Born to Die tour.

eras.label: Honeymoon
eras.title: Honeymoon in slow motion
eras.summary: A longer, slower record; a tour that widened the stage; a brief detour into someone else's album.
eras.lede: Honeymoon arrived on 18 September 2015: fourteen tracks, 65 minutes, and a deliberate step back toward the baroque pop of Born to Die after the guitar-heavy Ultraviolence. It was produced by Del Rey with Rick Nowels and Kieron Menzies.

sections.heading: The record
body: The album opens with the title track and moves through “Music to Watch Boys To”, “Terrence Loves You”, “High by the Beach”, “Freak”, and “The Blackest Day”. “Burnt Norton” sets a passage of T. S. Eliot over an interlude; “Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood” closes the record.

It peaked at number two on the Billboard 200 and reached the top five in more than twenty countries. The pace is deliberate: long intros, unhurried choruses, and a production that treats silence as part of the arrangement.

sections.heading: The tour
body: The Endless Summer Tour took the album across North America in 2015, with Courtney Love and Grimes on selected dates. In 2016, Del Rey appeared on the Weeknd's “Starboy”, a collaboration that pushed her voice into a different kind of pop production.
The Honeymoon photographs in this archive come from Sasquatch! 2015. They are wide, stage-lit images rather than close portraits — which suits an album that often keeps its narrator at a distance.

eras.label: Lust for Life
eras.title: Lust for Life and the open door
eras.summary: A brighter, collaborative record that put the audience in the room.
eras.lede: Lust for Life was released on 21 July 2017. It is the first Del Rey album that sounds like a group conversation: the Weeknd, A$AP Rocky, Playboi Carti, Stevie Nicks, and Sean Ono Lennon all pass through it.

sections.heading: A wider cast
body: The 16-track album includes “Love”, “Lust for Life”, “13 Beaches”, “Cherry”, “Summer Bummer”, “Groupie Love”, and “Get Free”. It topped the charts in twelve countries, including the US and the UK, and was nominated for Best Pop Vocal Album at the 60th Grammy Awards.

The collaborations are not decorations. They change the temperature of the record: the Weeknd duet is sleek and nocturnal, the Stevie Nicks track is weathered and generous, and the A$AP Rocky features push the album toward a more fragmented, contemporary pop sound.

sections.heading: The visual turn
body: The “Love” video, directed by Rich Lee, set the album's promotional tone: wide-screen, retro-futurist, and less confined to the noir interiors of the previous era. The cover art, with Del Rey smiling in front of a truck, was a small but deliberate break from the earlier iconography.
In the archive, Lust for Life is the hinge between the mid-2010s noir and the warmer, more collaborative records that follow. The 2017 festival photographs catch that shift in daylight.

eras.label: Norman Fucking Rockwell!
eras.title: Norman Fucking Rockwell! and the long exhale
eras.summary: Jack Antonoff, Laurel Canyon light, and the record that many critics treat as her best.
eras.lede: Norman Fucking Rockwell! was released on 30 August 2019. The first full album with Jack Antonoff as a central collaborator, it traded some of the earlier maximalism for soft rock, piano, and a slower, more conversational kind of songwriting.

sections.heading: The record
body: The 14-track album includes “Mariners Apartment Complex”, “Venice Bitch”, “Fuck It I Love You”, “Doin' Time”, “Cinnamon Girl”, “The Greatest”, and “Hope Is a Dangerous Thing for a Woman Like Me to Have – but I Have It”.

It reached number one in seven countries, including the UK, and number three in the US. It was nominated for Album of the Year at the 62nd Grammy Awards and later entered Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time.

sections.heading: Why it lasts
body: The album's reputation rests on restraint: long songs that do not rush, lyrics that leave space around the joke, and arrangements that sound like a room rather than a set. It is the chapter where the archive's earlier threads — Hollywood, Americana, self-mythology — become something closer to conversation.

The only NFR photograph in the collection is from the Grammy Museum in October 2019. It is a close, low-light image, which is appropriate for an album that often feels like it is being sung just out of frame.

eras.label: Chemtrails / Blue Banisters
eras.title: Chemtrails, Blue Banisters, and the quiet house
eras.summary: Two albums in seven months, plus a poetry book and a spoken-word record: the most domestic, reflective stretch of the catalogue.
eras.lede: In 2020, Del Rey published Violet Bent Backwards over the Grass, a poetry collection with a companion spoken-word album. Chemtrails over the Country Club followed on 19 March 2021; Blue Banisters arrived on 22 October 2021, only seven months later.

sections.heading: Violet
body: The spoken-word album, produced with Jack Antonoff, sets 14 poems against sparse piano and strings. It is not a pop record, and it is not meant to be: it is the clearest statement of Del Rey as a writer working in a different register.

The book and the album are related but separate releases. The book arrived in September 2020; the album had come out in July. The archive lists them together because they share a voice and a moment, not because they are the same object.

sections.heading: Two albums
body: Chemtrails is a folk, country-folk, and Americana record with contributions from Nikki Lane, Weyes Blood, and Zella Day. It debuted at number one in eight countries, including the UK, and number two in the US.

Blue Banisters is looser and more self-referential, with “Text Book”, “Blue Banisters”, “Arcadia”, “Dealer”, and “Wildflower Wildfire”; it reached number eight in the US and number one in Argentina and the Netherlands. The two records are often discussed together because they arrived so close together, but they are different rooms in the same house.

eras.label: Ocean Blvd
eras.title: Ocean Blvd and the tunnel
eras.summary: A long, dense album about family, memory, and the stories we build around both.
eras.lede: Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd was released on 24 March 2023. At 16 tracks and nearly 78 minutes, it is one of Del Rey's densest records, with production from Jack Antonoff, Drew Erickson, Zach Dawes, and others.

sections.heading: The record
body: The album includes “The Grants”, “A&W”, “Candy Necklace”, “Kintsugi”, “Fingertips”, “Paris, Texas”, “Let the Light In”, and “Taco Truck x VB”. It features Jon Batiste, Bleachers, Father John Misty, Tommy Genesis, SYML, and Riopy.
It topped charts in eight countries and reached number three in the US. The album received nominations for Album of the Year and Best Alternative Music Album at the 66th Grammy Awards.

sections.heading: Before and after
body: In 2022, “Snow on the Beach”, a collaboration with Taylor Swift, became Del Rey's highest-charting entry on the Billboard Hot 100 at the time. In 2023, “Say Yes to Heaven” — a song recorded a decade earlier — was finally released officially.

Ocean Blvd is the archive's longest chapter by runtime and the one that most rewards a linear listen. The MITA photograph in the collection is a wide, black-and-white crowd shot: a reminder that these songs about memory were also performed in rooms full of people.

eras.label: Stove
eras.title: Stove and the next chapter
eras.summary: A country record announced under three titles, delayed, expanded, and still not out — plus a companion album and a handful of singles.
eras.lede: The next chapter has been public for longer than most albums. In January 2024, Del Rey announced a country project called Lasso; by November 2024 it had become The Right Person Will Stay, and in August 2025 she confirmed the title Stove. As of 24 November 2026, the album has not been released.

sections.heading: The singles
body: “Henry, Come On” arrived on 11 April 2025, followed by “Bluebird” on 18 April 2025 and “White Feather Hawk Tail Deer Hunter” on 17 February 2026. At Stagecoach in April 2025, she performed three new songs — “Stars Fell on Alabama”, “Quiet in the South”, and “57.5” — that were expected to appear on the album.

The release has moved more than once. It was first expected in September 2024, then May 2025, then early 2026. Del Rey has said the delay came from adding new material; some of that material eventually became a separate companion album.

sections.heading: The wider frame
body: In 2024, “Tough” with Quavo was released. In 2026, Del Rey was announced as the singer of the theme for the James Bond game 007 First Light, and she appeared on Zach Bryan's “Lies” in October.

On 15 July 2026, she announced that additional material from the Stove sessions had become a separate companion album. The vinyl artwork suggested the title Spyda, but no final title or release date has been confirmed. This chapter is deliberately marked as open: the archive will not pretend that an unreleased record has a finished shape.

albums.title: Kill Kill
albums.label: 5 Points
albums.summary: The first public record: three songs, 13 minutes, and a name that would not last.
narrative: Kill Kill was released on 21 October 2008 under the name Lizzy Grant. Produced by David Kahne, the three-track EP introduces the torch-song register and the trailer-park imagery that would become more legible later.

It is a small record, but it is the archive's starting point. The title track, “Yayo”, and “Gramma (Blue Ribbon Sparkler Trailer Heaven)” already contain the ingredients — the cinematic frame, the worn glamour, the slight remove from the present — that the later albums would amplify.
albums.tracklistNote: Three tracks. The EP was later included in full on the 2010 album Lana Del Ray.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Out of print; not on major streaming services

albums.title: Lana Del Ray
albums.label: 5 Points
albums.summary: The debut album under the Lizzy Grant name: 13 tracks, a different spelling, and a record that disappeared from sale soon after.
narrative: Lana Del Ray — note the spelling — was released on 4 January 2010 through 5 Points Records. Produced by David Kahne, it collects 13 songs, including new versions of “Kill Kill”, “Gramma”, and “Yayo”.

The album was withdrawn from digital retail after Del Rey signed with a major label; it remains the clearest document of the pre-“Video Games” project. The title is sometimes written Lana Del Ray and sometimes Lana Del Rey; the album cover uses Ray.

albums.title: Born to Die
albums.label: Stranger / Interscope / Polydor
albums.producers: Emile Haynie; Patrik Berger; Justin Parker; Robopop; Rick Nowels; Al Shux
albums.summary: The major-label debut: 12 tracks in its standard edition, a deluxe edition with three more, and a cinematic frame that became the template for the next decade.
narrative: Born to Die was released on 27 January 2012. Its standard edition runs 12 tracks, from “Born to Die” and “Off to the Races” to “Summertime Sadness” and “This Is What Makes Us Girls”; the deluxe edition adds “Without You”, “Lolita”, and “Lucky Ones”.

The album peaked at number two on the Billboard 200 and topped charts in Australia, France, Germany, and the UK, among others. By December 2025, it had spent 618 weeks on the Billboard 200 — the longest run by a female artist in the chart's history, according to Billboard.
The Paradise Edition reissue, released on 9 November 2012, combines the standard album with the eight-track Paradise EP.

albums.tracklistNote: Standard edition. The deluxe edition adds “Without You”, “Lolita”, and “Lucky Ones”.

albums.title: Lana Del Rey
albums.label: Stranger
albums.producers: Emile Haynie; Justin Parker; Robopop; Patrik Berger
albums.summary: A four-track introduction released just before the debut album.
narrative: The Lana Del Rey EP was released on 10 January 2012 through Stranger Records. Its four tracks — “Video Games”, “Born to Die”, “Blue Jeans”, and “Off to the Races” — are the clearest early statement of the project's range: one homemade hit, one widescreen ballad, one noir guitar song, and one rap-adjacent curveball.
It is not the same release as the 2010 album Lana Del Ray. The shared name is one of the reasons the early discography needs a careful timeline.

albums.title: Paradise
albums.label: Polydor / Interscope
albums.producers: Rick Nowels; Justin Parker; Rick Rubin; Emile Haynie
albums.summary: Eight tracks of widescreen Americana, plus the iTunes bonus “Burning Desire”.
narrative: Paradise was released on 9 November 2012. Its eight tracks include “Ride”, “American”, “Cola”, “Body Electric”, “Blue Velvet”, “Gods & Monsters”, “Yayo”, and “Bel Air”; the iTunes edition added “Burning Desire”.
It debuted at number ten on the Billboard 200 and was later packaged with Born to Die as The Paradise Edition. The EP is the most direct bridge between the debut album and the Tropico film.
albums.tracklistNote: Eight standard tracks plus the iTunes bonus “Burning Desire”.

albums.title: Tropico
albums.label: Interscope / Polydor
albums.producers: Rick Nowels; Dan Heath; Emile Haynie; Tim Larcombe
albums.summary: A 27-minute short film built around three Paradise songs.
narrative: Tropico is a 27-minute short film directed by Anthony Mandler, premiered in December 2013. It is structured in three chapters — “Body Electric”, “Gods & Monsters”, and “Bel Air” — and frames the songs as a loose Adam-and-Eve narrative.

It is not a standalone album, but it belongs in the release chronology because it is the era's most complete visual statement. The film is listed here as a film/soundtrack release, not a studio album.

albums.summary: 11 tracks of live guitar, desert rock, and a harder vocal edge.
narrative: Ultraviolence was released on 13 June 2014. Produced largely with Dan Auerbach, its 11-track standard edition moves from “Cruel World” to “The Other Woman”, with “West Coast”, “Brooklyn Baby”, and “Shades of Cool” at the centre.

It debuted at number one in eleven countries, including the US, and reached the top five in more than twenty territories. The deluxe edition adds “Black Beauty”, “Guns and Roses”, and “Florida Kilos”; the iTunes edition adds “Is This Happiness”, and the Japanese/Target edition adds “Flipside”.

narrative: Honeymoon was released on 18 September 2015. Produced by Del Rey with Rick Nowels and Kieron Menzies, it marked a departure from the guitar-driven Ultraviolence and a return to the baroque pop of Born to Die and Paradise.

The album opens with the title track and moves through “Music to Watch Boys To”, “Terrence Loves You”, “High by the Beach”, “Freak”, and “The Blackest Day”. It peaked at number two on the Billboard 200 and reached the top five in more than twenty countries.
The Endless Summer Tour followed in 2015, with Courtney Love and Grimes on selected dates. In 2016, Del Rey appeared on the Weeknd's “Starboy”.

The album topped the charts in twelve countries, including the US and the UK, and was nominated for Best Pop Vocal Album at the 60th Grammy Awards. Its 16 tracks include “Love”, “Lust for Life”, “13 Beaches”, “Cherry”, “Summer Bummer”, “Groupie Love”, and “Get Free”.

It reached number one in seven countries, including the UK, and number three in the US. It was nominated for Album of the Year at the 62nd Grammy Awards and later entered Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time.

albums.title: Violet Bent Backwards over the Grass
albums.label: Interscope / Polydor
albums.summary: A poetry collection and a companion spoken-word album: 14 poems, sparse piano, and a different kind of attention.
narrative: Violet Bent Backwards over the Grass began as a poetry collection, published by Simon & Schuster on 29 September 2020. The companion spoken-word album arrived earlier, on 28 July 2020, through Interscope and Polydor, with music by Jack Antonoff.

Its 14 tracks are poems, not songs; the record is best approached as a reading rather than a pop album. The book and the album are related but separate releases, and the archive lists them together because they share a voice and a moment.

narrative: Chemtrails over the Country Club was released on 19 March 2021. Del Rey enlisted Jack Antonoff as her co-producer for most of the album, with Rick Nowels producing one track; the record features Nikki Lane, Weyes Blood, and Zella Day.

It debuted at number one in eight countries, including the UK, and number two in the US. Its 11 tracks include “White Dress”, “Chemtrails over the Country Club”, “Tulsa Jesus Freak”, “Let Me Love You like a Woman”, “Yosemite”, and “For Free”.

albums.title: Blue Banisters
albums.label: Interscope / Polydor
albums.producers: Lana Del Rey; Gabe Simon; Zachary Dawes; Drew Erickson; Dean Reid; Loren Humphrey; Mike Dean; Barrie-James O'Neill; Rick Nowels
albums.summary: A loose, self-referential 15-track album released seven months after Chemtrails.
narrative: Blue Banisters was released on 22 October 2021, seven months after Chemtrails over the Country Club. It was produced by Del Rey with Zachary Dawes, Drew Erickson, Loren Humphrey, Mike Dean, Barrie-James O'Neill, Rick Nowels, and others.

The 15-track album includes “Text Book”, “Blue Banisters”, “Arcadia”, “Black Bathing Suit”, “Dealer”, and “Wildflower Wildfire”. It peaked at number eight on the Billboard 200 and reached number one in Argentina and the Netherlands.

albums.title: Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd
albums.label: Interscope / Polydor
albums.producers: Lana Del Rey; Mike Hermosa; Jack Antonoff; Drew Erickson; Zach Dawes; Benji Lysaght
albums.summary: A 16-track, 78-minute album about family, memory, and the stories we build around both.
narrative: Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd was released on 24 March 2023. It features production by Del Rey, Mike Hermosa, Jack Antonoff, Drew Erickson, Zach Dawes, and Benji Lysaght, and collaborations with Jon Batiste, Bleachers, Father John Misty, Tommy Genesis, SYML, and Riopy.

The album includes “The Grants”, “A&W”, “Candy Necklace”, “Kintsugi”, “Fingertips”, “Paris, Texas”, “Let the Light In”, and “Taco Truck x VB”. It topped charts in eight countries and reached number three in the US.
It was nominated for Album of the Year and Best Alternative Music Album at the 66th Grammy Awards. In 2023, “Say Yes to Heaven” — a song recorded a decade earlier — was finally released officially.

albums.title: Stove
albums.label: Interscope / Polydor
albums.producers: Lana Del Rey; Jack Antonoff; Drew Erickson; Luke Laird
albums.summary: The tenth studio album: a country project announced under three titles, delayed, and still pending as of 24 November 2026.
narrative: Stove was first announced in January 2024 as Lasso, then renamed The Right Person Will Stay in November 2024, and finally confirmed as Stove in August 2025. It is described as a country record, though Del Rey has said it is not a heavy departure from her previous work.

Three singles have been released: “Henry, Come On” (11 April 2025), “Bluebird” (18 April 2025), and “White Feather Hawk Tail Deer Hunter” (17 February 2026). At Stagecoach in April 2025, she performed three new songs — “Stars Fell on Alabama”, “Quiet in the South”, and “57.5” — that were expected to appear on the album.
The album was not released in early 2026 as originally planned. No official tracklist or final release date has been announced. This page will be updated when both are confirmed.

fanNotes.title: Notes from the archive
fanNotes.lede: A public-facing notebook about why this archive exists, how it is made, and what it refuses to do. It is written for readers, not kept as a private diary.

notes.title: Why this archive exists
body: [Archive keeper: add a short note about why you started this archive, what you want it to be for other fans, and what you would like to add next.]
This space is reserved for the person who maintains the site. Write for readers who arrive without context, not for a private diary.

notes.title: How a photograph earns its place
body: Every image in the archive is downloaded and stored locally. Nothing is hotlinked from a search engine. Each photo has a named creator, a link to its original file page, a licence, and a link to the licence terms.

If a photo's licence cannot be established, it is not used. Two eras currently use a placeholder instead of an uncredited image: the earliest Lizzy Grant years and the Chemtrails / Blue Banisters period. That is a deliberate limit, not an oversight.

notes.title: A note on corrections
body: This is a fan archive, not a newsroom. Facts are checked against Wikipedia's cited sources and, where possible, the primary announcement. Date-sensitive claims — especially anything about Stove — are marked with the date they were checked.

If something is wrong, the fix is to correct it in the data source and rebuild, not to quietly patch the HTML. The archive is generated from one JSON file, so a correction propagates to every page that uses it.

rules: No gossip, and no speculation about private life.
No fabricated quotes, and no full lyrics.
No photograph without a named creator, source, and licence.
No claim about an unreleased record that is not marked as provisional.

submit.title: Have a correction or a licensed photograph?
submit.body: Corrections, takedown requests, and licensed photograph offers are handled through a public issue on the project repository. No email address has been invented.

about.title: A fan archive, with receipts
about.lede: Lizzy to Lana is an independent fan archive of Lana Del Rey's recorded work. It is built and maintained by a fan, for other fans.

sections.heading: What this is
body: A multi-page reference for the eras, releases, and a small photo collection. Every page is generated from one JSON source; every photo has a credit and a licence.

The site is deliberately quiet. There is no autoplay, no tracking script, no comment section, and no infinite feed. The goal is to make the records easier to follow, not to compete with the official channels.

sections.heading: What this is not
body: Not an official site. Not a news site. Not a diary. Not a lyrics database. Not a gossip page.
It does not speculate about private life, publish unverified claims, or reproduce full lyrics. Short quotations are used only where they are attributed and necessary.

sections.heading: Editorial policy
body: Facts are checked against Wikipedia's cited sources and, where possible, the primary announcement. Date-sensitive claims — especially anything about Stove — are marked with the date they were checked.
Unreleased records are described as provisional. If a tracklist, title, or release date has not been confirmed, the page says so instead of filling the gap.

sections.heading: Photo policy
body: Photographs are downloaded from Wikimedia Commons, stored locally, and served in responsive AVIF, WebP, and JPEG variants. Each image is credited to its creator, linked to its original file page, and used under a named Creative Commons licence.
If a licence cannot be established, the archive uses a placeholder. Two periods currently have no licensed photograph: the earliest Lizzy Grant years and the Chemtrails / Blue Banisters era.

sections.heading: Takedown and corrections
body: If you are the rights holder for an image and believe it has been used incorrectly, contact the address below with the file URL and the licence concern. The image will be removed or corrected promptly.
The same address is the right place to send a factual correction. No contact email has been invented; the placeholder will be replaced before the site is promoted publicly.

colophon: Static HTML, CSS, and a small amount of JavaScript. Built with a Node script; images and OG cards are generated with Python and Pillow.
Fonts: Cormorant Garamond, Inter, and Homemade Apple, self-hosted under the SIL Open Font License.
Search: Pagefind, generated at build time and run entirely in the browser.
Hosting: a private VPS running nginx, with HTTPS, gzip, long-lived caching for hashed assets, and a small set of security headers.

search.note: Search covers the text of every page. Photographs are indexed through their captions and credits on the gallery and era pages.
